newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo to ready plan to release frozen savings.
newsitem.headline: Yugo to ready plan to release frozen savings.

text.p: Yugoslavia's government will outline its proposal on paying back over $4 billion in old hard currency savings frozen since 1991 to its holders by the end of 1997, a senior government official said on Thursday.

"It's high time we dealt with the issue and the government should come up with its proposal by the end of the year," recently appointed Yugoslav Finance Minister Bozidar Gazivoda told Reuters in an interview.
The federal government must find ways to service those savings, said Gazivoda, still an outgoing central bank deputy governor waiting for Serbia and Montenegro to come to terms over his successor.
But he could not say when the first payments would begin. "We have minimum financial means." he added
Gazivoda said Yugoslavia, now comprising Serbia and Montenegro, will resort to various mechanisms of raising funds to service its debt to the population.
Yugoslavia will need some fresh external borrowing, but also must use privatisation receipts to service the debt and exploit fiscal mechanisms to some extent, he said.
But the minister rejected any possibility of servicing the debt through fiscal instruments and via inflation.

"In case of privatisation, we must give an absolute priority to holders of old hard currency savings in buying stake in state-controlled companies because they invested cash which was spent for the needs of this economy.

"It is clear that frozen savings are a liability which must be cleared, and there is no difference between those savings and the country's external debt. We owe money and shall seek solutions in that respect," Gazivoda said.
The minister insisted repayment of 6.8 billion German marks of savings and accrued interest was not the sole responsibility of the federal government and its budget.
"Both Serbia and Montenegro must take part in it and provide funds for debt servicing. We must jointly seek a way out."
Gazivoda regretted that depositors' associations rejected the government's proposal to transform entire frozen savings to public debt.

Dealing with frozen savings, with the state taking over responsibility from commercial banks, was also seen as a way to clear banks of huge debts to the population and prepare them for a rehabilitation programme.

Economists said release of frozen deposits was the key for returning savings to domestic banks, whose fixed term dinar deposits stood at 118.1 million dinars ($21.4 million) at the end of 1996 and accounted for 0.15 percent of Yugoslavia's GDP.
"Banks frequently use frozen savings issue as an excuse for their daily problems and for not behaving in a market manner," Gazivoda said.

The National Bank of Yugoslavia has spent 600 million dinars to service frozen savings since 1994. "But it was the base money that financed the debt not the so-called real sources," he said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
